items.question: Why isn't Lake Powell filling back up?
items.answer: Two forces hold it down. The Colorado River basin is in its driest 20-plus-year stretch in roughly 1,200 years, so far less water flows in than last century's average. At the same time the river is over-allocated, with demand outrunning supply. Wet years help, but the structural deficit keeps pulling the reservoir down between them.

Lake Powell’s water levels remain under pressure heading into summer after a disappointing snow season across much of the Colorado River Basin, raising fresh concerns about water supplies in the Colorado River System, one of the nation’s most important river systems.

The timing is especially problematic because the annual runoff season is largely coming to an end. Water managers typically rely on melting mountain snow during spring and early summer to provide the largest inflows of the year to Lake Powell and downstream reservoirs.

Lake Powell is the second-largest man-made reservoir in the United States, formed by the Glen Canyon Dam on the Colorado River in Utah near the Arizona border. With a capacity of 24.3 million acre-feet at full pool (elevation 3,700 ft), Lake Powell serves as a key storage facility for the Upper Colorado River Basin states.

Like its downstream partner Lake Mead, Lake Powell has been significantly impacted by the ongoing Colorado River drought. The minimum power pool elevation is 3,490 feet, below which Glen Canyon Dam cannot generate hydroelectric power.
Lake Powell (24.3M acre-feet, Glen Canyon Dam) is upstream of Lake Mead (26.1M acre-feet, Hoover Dam) on the Colorado River. Water released from Powell flows into Mead.
